column4: God “gave each thing its creation, then guided” (أَعْطَىٰ ... ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ), reproducing the section’s sequence of the giving hand and the guidance-gift.
God gives and removes sovereignty, raises and lowers, while “good is in Your hand” (بِيَدِكَ ٱلْخَيْرُ); one verse gathers the section’s divine hand, gift-as-khayr, giving, and taking from above.
The charge that God’s hand is bound is answered with “His two hands are outspread” (يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ) and He spends as He wills, making the open divine hand explicit.
Solomon contrasts the envoys’ gift with what God has given him and says they rejoice in their gift; هَدِيَّتِكُمْ meets divine giving and tests whether a hand-to-hand offering is truly enriching.
God gives from all that people ask of Him, then His favor proves uncountable; asking, fulfilled need, giving, and niʿma occur in one movement.

The proper response to distribution is satisfaction with what God and His messenger gave and hope that God “will give us” from His bounty, closely matching gift followed by contentment in 93:5 and correcting 9:58.
“This is Our gift” (هَٰذَا عَطَآؤُنَا) leaves Solomon free to give or withhold, explicitly passing the giver’s hand into a human hand.
God tells Moses, “You have been granted your request” (أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ), exactly enacting the source dictionary’s sense of meeting an asker’s need.
Moses names himself needy for any khayr God sends down; the supplicant below awaits good as a gift descending from the divine hand.
A commanded remembrance of God’s favor recounts enemies stretching out their hands and God restraining them, joining niʿma to the prevention of a wrongful reaching hand.
A question about what to give is answered with whatever khayr is spent for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler; asking, gift-as-good, and the protected recipients meet directly.
The people ask for a ruling about women and orphan girls whose prescribed due they do not give, so سؤال and the withholding hand converge around the orphan’s right.
When orphans and needy people attend an estate division, the heirs must provide for them from it and speak fitting words, pairing the giving hand with the speaking mouth.
The command to hand orphans their property and not consume it with one’s own property directly reverses the overpowering hand that takes without the orphan’s consent.
Guardians must test orphans, hand over their property at maturity, avoid consuming it wastefully, and take witnesses; it measures precisely when the upper hand must open and withdraw.
The asker and the deprived possess a right within the believers’ wealth, so the open palm is met as a rights-bearing hand rather than an intrusion.
Their wealth contains “a known right,” establishing that the giver’s transfer in 70:25 is an obligation with a measure, not arbitrary generosity.
The known right belongs “to the asker and the deprived” (لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ), repeating the pairing in 51:19 and including the need that remains unspoken.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor spread to its furthest extent, giving the section’s open hand an explicit measure and boundary.
If one must turn away while awaiting provision from God, one must still speak gently; the unavailable gift is replaced by a fitting word rather than rebuffing the asker.
When people ask what to spend, the answer is “the surplus” (ٱلْعَفْوَ), turning the second sense of سؤال into a measure for the giving hand.
Restrained needy people are mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not ask insistently, making visible the deprived hand that never opens and still has a claim.
A fitting word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by hurt; speech can honor the receiving hand when a material gift does not.
Those who spend must not follow what their hands give with reminder or injury, setting a boundary between recounting God’s favor and boasting of one’s own favor.
Givers must spend from good things and not select what they themselves would accept only with closed eyes, forcing the donor to imagine the receiving hand.
True piety includes giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, askers, and captives; both orphan and open-palmed asker stand before the same giving hand.
The righteous give food they love to the needy person, orphan, and captive, staging the transfer to two recipients central to the section.
They seek neither repayment nor thanks from those they feed, keeping the gift from becoming a hand-to-hand bargain for praise.
“Feeding on a day of hunger” supplies the concrete act whose receiving figures are named in the next two ayat.
The first recipient of that feeding is an orphan of kin, directly answering the section’s demand that the stronger hand protect the orphan.
The second recipient is a destitute person in the dust, giving bodily form to the deprived person whose need may or may not be voiced.
“We have given you al-Kawthar” (أَعْطَيْنَٰكَ ٱلْكَوْثَرَ) is the completed divine gift to the same prophetic addressee promised satisfaction in 93:5.
God extends provision to both worldly-seeking groups and says the Lord’s gift (عَطَآءُ رَبِّكَ) is not barred, displaying the reach of the giving hand.
The people made happy receive “a gift uncut” (عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ), clarifying how divine giving can remain rather than pass away.
The one who “gives and is mindful” (أَعْطَىٰ وَٱتَّقَىٰ) is the praised human giving hand immediately before this surah.
The queen sends a هَدِيَّة and waits to see what the messengers return with, staging the source dictionary’s gift carried from one friendly hand to another.
All bounty is said to be in God’s hand, and He gives it to whom He wills; the metaphorical giver named by the section is made explicit.
The People of the Book are told that bounty is in God’s hand and He gives it as He wills, again locating provision in the divine hand rather than human control.
In the pledge, “God’s hand is above their hands” (يَدُ ٱللَّهِ فَوْقَ أَيْدِيهِمْ); a covenantal hand-to-hand act makes palpable the section’s meeting between the hand above and hands below.
God “takes the charities” (يَأْخُذُ ٱلصَّدَقَٰتِ), reversing the ordinary direction of giving as the divine hand above receives what the human hand offers.
A good loan to God is received and returned many times over while God constricts and expands, turning giving into an exchange whose increase comes from above.
The one who lends God a good loan receives it multiplied and a noble reward, a hand-to-hand exchange in which the divine return surpasses the human gift.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, showing the giver becoming a receiver from the One to whom the gift was offered.
God purchases believers’ lives and wealth in exchange for the Garden and calls this covenant a sale, making the section’s “exchange between hands” an explicit transaction.
A gift intended to grow in other people’s wealth does not grow with God, whereas alms seeking God’s face multiply; the recipient and purpose determine what a transfer becomes.
The servants’ spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but a measured middle, paralleling the bounded opening of the hand in 17:29.
Each person spends according to what God has given, and God promises ease after hardship; the human hand’s measure is set by the prior divine gift.
People count their submission as a favor to the Prophet, but God says His favor is that He guided them; niʿma/minna, telling, and guidance are disentangled in one correction.
Believers are commanded to remember God’s favor upon them together with the revealed Book and wisdom, a close counterpart to speaking of the Lord’s niʿma.
The command to remember God’s favor identifies former enemies whose hearts He joined, turning an unseen divine gift into a narrated social transformation.
The command to remember God’s favor is joined to remembering the covenant they voiced, linking received niʿma with spoken acknowledgment.
Moses tells his people to remember God’s favor in making prophets and rulers among them and giving them what others had not received.
Moses is told to remind his people of God’s favor in rescuing them from Pharaoh, another explicit movement from a saving divine act to verbal remembrance.
Believers must remember God’s favor when unseen forces drove off the armies, so an invisible protecting hand becomes something recounted.
People are commanded to remember God’s favor and asked whether any creator besides God provides for them, fastening the spoken favor to its sole giving source.
God’s favors cannot be counted, matching 14:34 and explaining why the commanded telling of favor cannot exhaust the gift.
Every favor people possess is from God, and distress makes them cry to Him, joining the origin of the gift to the supplicant’s upward appeal.
People recognize God’s favor and then deny it, the direct failure of acknowledgment against which the command to speak of the Lord’s favor stands.
God has lavished favors both outward and inward, extending the section’s visible hand-gift to provision that remains hidden.
“We have given you” the seven repeated verses and the great Qur’an is another completed divine grant addressed directly to the Prophet.
After naming revelation and teaching given to the Prophet, the ayah says God’s favor upon him is immense, supplying concrete content for speaking of his Lord’s favor.
Those who criticize the distribution are satisfied if “they are given” (أُعْطُوا) and angry if not; it is a corrupt mirror of the Lord giving until the Prophet is satisfied.

God is “the Overpowering above His servants” (ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ), matching the dictionary’s qahr from above while marking the boundary between divine sovereignty and a human overpowering an orphan.
The repeated title “the Overpowering above His servants” precedes the taking of souls by messengers, again reserving legitimate qahr from above to God.
Thamud call their companion, who reaches out (فَتَعَاطَىٰ) and hamstrings the she-camel; the same root’s taking hand becomes seizure of what was not his by right.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are in fact consuming fire, exposing what the descending, taking hand does to itself.
The condemned person “gave a little and withheld” (أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًۭا وَأَكْدَىٰ), placing the root’s giving motion beside the hand that abruptly closes.
Hypocrites command wrong, forbid right, and “close their hands” (يَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ), bodily reversing the open giving hand.
When called to spend, some withhold; the ayah answers that the withholder harms only himself because God is rich and humans are needy.
People of bounty and means must not swear to stop giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants, so pardon reopens a hand that grievance had closed.
The command not to confer a favor in order to get more prevents the gift from becoming a self-enriching claim over the recipient.
Pharaoh calls Moses’ upbringing a favor while suppressing Israel; Moses’ reply exposes a “favor” recounted by an oppressor as a claim of ownership.
“You do not honor the orphan” names the social posture opposite the prohibition against overpowering the orphan.
The same people do not urge one another to feed the needy, showing a community that keeps every giving hand closed.
They devour inheritance voraciously, continuing the orphan context with the image of a stronger party consuming another’s due.
The denier is the one who violently repels the orphan, an enacted opposite of “do not overpower the orphan.”
He does not urge feeding the needy, extending the repulsed orphan scene into refusal to mobilize any giving hand.
The frown and turning away supply the bodily opposite of receiving a vulnerable petitioner without rebuke.
The blind man’s arrival identifies the vulnerable person from whom the response in 80:1 turned away.
The other side of the episode is the person who comes striving toward the Prophet, giving direction and effort to the petitioner’s approach.
His fear makes clear the sincere need behind that approach rather than a claim on worldly rank.
Being distracted from that sincere visitor completes the cautionary scene opposite the command not to rebuff the asker.
Abel says that even if his brother stretches a hand to kill him, he will not stretch his own hand back, contrasting the wrongful reaching hand with deliberate restraint.
Enemies stretch their hands and tongues toward believers with evil, coupling hostile hand and hostile speech where the section joins beneficent hand and speech.
Charity is nullified by reminders and injury, like a bare rock whose soil is stripped by rain; the transferred object cannot excuse domination of the recipient.
Property may not be consumed wrongfully; only trade by mutual consent is allowed, setting consent as the boundary between exchange and the section’s taking of what is not one’s right.
Approaching an orphan’s property is forbidden except in the best manner until maturity, sharply limiting the guardian’s upper hand.
The same ban on approaching orphan property except beneficially lasts until maturity, and the covenant must be fulfilled.
God sends the she-camel as a trial and commands watchful patience, introducing the living object toward which the wrongful hand will reach in 54:29.
Water is to be divided and each share attended in turn, establishing the she-camel’s allotted right before the seizure in 54:29.
Thamud hamstring the she-camel and defiantly demand punishment, another telling of the very act performed by the reaching companion in 54:29.
After they hamstring her, Salih announces their three-day respite, carrying the wrongful reach into its promised consequence.
Salih states that the she-camel has her drink and the people theirs on an appointed day, specifying the right violated by the later hand.
They are forbidden to touch her with harm, stating the boundary immediately before they cross it.
They hamstring her and become regretful, repeating the dark reaching-and-taking scene with its inward consequence.
God’s messenger warns them concerning “God’s she-camel and her drink,” again naming both the protected creature and her right.
They deny the messenger and hamstring her, after which their Lord crushes them for the sin; the hand that overpowered the vulnerable meets overpowering judgment.
Salih tells Thamud to let God’s she-camel eat on God’s earth and not touch her with harm, supplying the protected freedom behind 7:77’s violation.
Salih similarly calls her God’s she-camel, lets her feed, and forbids harmful touch, defining what the taking hand had no right to seize.
Yusuf contrasts many divided lords with “God, the One, the Overpowering”; the title locates qahr in undivided divine authority rather than human mastery of the weak.
After affirming God as creator of everything, the ayah names Him the One, the Overpowering, grounding qahr in universal creation rather than social power.
All creation emerges before God, the One, the Overpowering, placing qahr in the final leveling where no human upper hand remains.
The messenger declares no deity but God, the One, the Overpowering, making qahr part of exclusive divinity rather than a license for human domination.
The One, the Overpowering is above the imagined choice of offspring, again attaching the root to God’s incomparable sovereignty.
On the day when nothing is hidden, dominion belongs to God, the One, the Overpowering; every temporary human upper hand has disappeared.
Israel is commanded to remember the favor God bestowed and to fulfill its covenant, making received niʿma answerable in memory and conduct.
The repeated command to remember God’s favor addresses a people collectively, a communal counterpart to telling of one’s Lord’s favor.
The command to remember the favor is repeated at the close of the Israel passage, showing that divine gifts remain claims on the recipient’s speech and conduct.
People must eat the good lawful provision God gave and thank His favor, connecting the received thing to verbal acknowledgment.
Abraham is grateful for God’s favors, and God chooses and guides him, bringing favor and guidance together as the recipient’s gratitude answers the gift.
God grants female children to whom He wills and male children to whom He wills, presenting life itself as a discretionary gift from His hand.
He joins sons and daughters or makes whom He wills barren, completing 42:49’s picture of giving with a boundary no human hand controls.
All people are the needy ones toward God while God is self-sufficient, identifying every apparently giving human hand as fundamentally a receiving hand.
Whatever good believers spend returns fully to them, while guidance remains God’s affair; giving, return, and guidance are distinguished but held together.
People do not attain full piety until they give from what they love, giving Quranic form to the dictionary’s gift carried as an act of birr.
At harvest, people must give the crop’s due yet not waste, joining a recipient’s right to a measured rather than limitless opening of the hand.
Guardians must provide and clothe dependants from protected property and speak fitting words, another joining of responsible provision with honorable speech.
A question about orphans is answered with reform as best and with guarded permission to mix affairs, showing that proximity to orphan property must serve rather than overpower them.
